newsitem.title: FRANCE: Horror in Algeria as village prepares to bury dead.
newsitem.headline: Horror in Algeria as village prepares to bury dead.

text.p: Survivors who fled the massacre of 31 friends and neighbours gathered in their tiny Algerian village on Thursday to bury them, witnesses said.
"They are preparing for the burials today, in the village," said one Algerian resident, contacted by telephone.
Among the victims of the attack over Tuesday night and early Wednesday were 11 women. All the dead had their throats cut and many were mutilated.
Three nights earlier, 10 women and three children were killed in a similar night of bloodshed.
Five years of conflict between security forces and Moslem fundamentalists has largely inured Algerians to violence.

But on Thursday, as detail emerged of the brutality of what Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour called the "ignoble savagery" perpetrated on "defenceless people", Algerians reacted with outrage and horror.
"I am leaving Sid el Kebir, for anywhere, provided there is more mercy there," a 14-year-old boy from the village said just hours after the raid, blamed by the authorities on Islamists.

He was echoing the sentiments expressed by other villagers who said that once their dead were buried they would leave their community, just six km (four miles) from the garrison town of Blida, south of Algiers, for ever.

"The (attacking) group was made up of more than 20 people. They invaded a first building. Nine people, including three women and man aged over 60, had their throats slit," said Liberte, under the headline "Bloodbath at Sid el Kebir".

The "terrorists" moved on. "Twenty-two people, including eight women, suffered the same fate," it said. "A little girl of two years is missing. Some bodies were so mutilated that the families could not identify them."
El Watan newspaper, quoting doctors, said the killers had used saws on the bodies to mutilate them.
"About 50 people, mainly women and children...fled on foot...These families are poor. Among the victims were masons, manual workers, farmers, but mainly the unemployed," it said.
"Only those who have completely lost the spirit of humanity, in a fanaticism of the mad, could commit such acts," El Watan said in an editorial.
One woman told Le Matin newspaper: "The village was left to itself, with its population at the mercy of terrorists."
Algeria's main secular opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed accused the army of devoting itself to shielding the country's rulers while paying only lip service to the security of ordinary Algerians.

"I believe the security policy implemented by the army nowadays is not in the people's interest. It has been proved in more than one case that the army has not intervened to protect villages", said Ait Ahmed in an interview with the London-based Arab newspaper al Hayat.

"So it appears from that, that the army security policy aims in the first place at protecting the people in power, their interests and economic facilities which are looked upon as a source for them to hold on in power, like gas and oil," he said.

Overshadowed by the Sid el Kebir killing, four more people from one family were killed the same night by "terrorists" -- Algerian officials' term for Moslem fundamentalists -- at the nearby village of Bouinan, Le Matin said.
Among the dead there was a pregnant woman, it said.

An estimated 50,000 people have been killed since conflict erupted shortly after the authorities, in January 1992, cancelled a general election in which the now-outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a commanding lead.
Fresh elections are planned for early next year.
The upsurge of attacks on civilians comes ahead of a referendum slated for November 28 to change the constitution and ensure parties based on religion are banned.
The last vote held in this country of 29 million people, for presidential elections last year, saw a huge security force deployment.

El Watan wrote on Thursday: "It is permissible to doubt the great assurance given by the authorities...the citizen knows that total security cannot be guaranteed. But it is difficult to accept that criminal groups take a village hostage and carried out the most abominable acts without a helping hand coming to the rescue of the victims."
